justification: Originality and depth: the article delivers exactly on its stated angle and on CONTENT_PLAN.md row 7's differentiator ('Builds a tiny container so the magic disappears'). It is not a description of DI in the abstract -- it builds MiniContainer, a genuinely working ~60-line reflection-based container (the class body from `sealed class MiniContainer : IDisposable` through its closing brace is 59 lines by direct count), registers all three lifetimes, resolves a real four-type diamond dependency graph with it, and shows the identical four booleans reproduced by the real Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection package immediately after. It then does something almost no introductory DI content does: constructs a live, running captive-dependency bug (a singleton IReceiptSender capturing a scoped IAuditLog) and shows the wrong audit-log id printed for the second scope, not just describes the anti-pattern. I fetched Microsoft's own guidelines.md, which documents the identical anti-pattern -- but only as a static, unnamed Foo(Bar bar) snippet with no program output; the article's version is concrete, runs, and is verified against a real .NET 10 execution, which is the article's genuine value-add over its own most authoritative cited source, let alone over typical blog-tutorial coverage of DI (which stops at 'here's how AddScoped/AddSingleton work' and rarely reproduces a captive-dependency failure at all). Sourcing: all 6 front-matter sources are real Microsoft Learn pages; I fetched all 6 directly and checked every quotation against live page text. All verified verbatim: 'a single instance of the service will be created' / 'a new instance of the service will be created for each scope' / 'a new instance of the service will be created every time it is requested' (ServiceLifetime enum table, exact); 'the IServiceScopeFactory is always registered as a singleton' (overview page, Scope scenarios section, exact); 'if the app requires singleton behavior, allow the service container to manage the service's lifetime... don't implement the singleton design pattern and provide code to dispose of the singleton' (service-lifetimes page, quoted in the source's own original sentence order, unlike a discrepancy the sibling factory-builder-singleton review flagged for the same source); 'difficult to unit test' / 'the app should use a mock or stub... which isn't possible with this approach' (overview page, exact, ellipsis correctly elides only the class name); the captive-dependency term-of-art attribution to Mark Seemann (guidelines.md, accurate, not fabricated); and, most easily missed, 'that scoped services never gets resolved from root provider' -- this exact ungrammatical phrase is a verbatim match to the `validateScopes` boolean parameter description on the BuildServiceProvider(IServiceCollection, Boolean) overload, correctly cited to source [5], not the ServiceProviderOptions.ValidateScopes property (source [6], correctly used instead for the separate ValidateOnBuild quote). Every inline citation index resolves to the correct front-matter source. Where the article restates a well-known point in its own words (the three costs of a hard-coded dependency; the definition of a captive dependency) it uses its own domain example (InvoiceService/SmtpReceiptSender, ConsoleAuditLog with numbered instances) rather than the source's example (Worker/MessageWriter, Foo/Bar) -- no reused running example, consistent with the editorial brief's rule 4. Sibling-duplication check: factory-builder-singleton.md (now published) owns the classic Singleton pattern in full -- thread-safe Lazy<T> construction, the OrderProcessor/EmailSender.Instance testability demonstration, and the AddSingleton-replaces-classic-Singleton narrative, with its own bad-singleton-test/good-singleton-test pair. This article's 'Lifetimes' section addresses the classic Singleton pattern in exactly one paragraph, purely to distinguish it from the container's Singleton lifetime ('the container's singleton lifetime, covered here, is a registration policy applied to an ordinary class that has no idea it is being shared'), explicitly defers the classic-pattern material to 'a companion article on creational patterns,' and neither builds nor critiques a static-Instance Singleton anywhere in its own code. Its own AddSingleton usage is scoped to different material entirely -- lifetime precision (transient/scoped/singleton together), the MiniContainer build, and the captive-dependency bug -- none of which factory-builder-singleton.md covers. The two articles' only common quoted phrase source (service-lifetimes.md) is cited for non-overlapping sentences in each ('singleton services must be thread safe' in the sibling vs. the transient/scoped/singleton definitions and the don't-implement-the-pattern guidance here). docs/crosslinks/oop-design/dependency-injection.md documents this boundary explicitly and accurately. No duplicate coverage found. No filler: opens with a concrete claim about InvoiceService's actual constructor, no restated title, no 'in this article,' no summary conclusion -- the piece ends inside a worked exercise solution. Headings are specific to content, not a repeated Introduction/Conclusion template, and the shape (hard-coded -> hand injection -> composition root -> lifetimes -> container -> framework -> bug -> fix) matches the plan's assigned shape B and is structurally distinct from both strategy-observer-decorator.md's three-pattern shape and factory-builder-singleton.md's four-pattern-comparison shape. Three exercises use three different forms (find-the-bug, predict-the-output, explain-and-compare), are placed mid-article rather than bunched at the end, and none leaks its output panel before the solution. Front matter is accurate and non-clickbait: the title ('from First Principles') and description name exactly what the piece does (hand-fix, ~60-line container, reproduce a captive-dependency bug in the real package) with no overselling, and both match CONTENT_PLAN.md row 7 verbatim.
